strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and increasingly timely question: whether data-agnostic Hadamard transforms, now standard in LLM quantization pipelines, can be replaced by provably optimal data-aware blockwise transforms, particularly for the emerging MXFP4/NVFP4 microscaling formats.

The central theoretical contribution — closed-form optimal (FP) and asymptotically optimal (INT) blockwise transforms for joint weight-activation quantization — is genuinely novel to the best of the reviewer's knowledge, and the derivation (Theorem 1, Eqs. 13-14 and 16-24) is carried through with reasonable rigor using Cauchy-Schwarz, Jensen, and von Neumann trace inequalities, with proofs for the supporting max inequalities in the appendix.

The insight that orthogonal transforms provably cannot reduce quantization error under the smooth FP error model (Eq. 15), while the non-orthogonal WUSH construction can, provides genuine understanding and cleanly explains when Hadamard helps (INT/MXFP4-like formats) and when it does not (NVFP4, where H is empirically worse than identity).

The empirical evidence consistently supports the practical claim: WUSH beats identity, random rotation, and Hadamard on layerwise RTN loss (Table 1) and achieves the best average recovery on LM Eval Harness and Platinumbench across four models and two FP4 formats (Table 2, Figures 1-4), with sensible ablations (WUS vs. WUSH isolating the Hadamard backbone).

The method is calibration-based and closed-form (Algorithm 1), requiring no training, which distinguishes it from learned-rotation approaches like SpinQuant/FlatQuant and makes it attractive in principle.
weaknesses: The 'provably optimal' claim rests on several nontrivial approximations that are not fully quantified: the first-order expansion in Eq. 7 discards the second-order cross term ε(T_W w)ᵀε(T_X x); the quantizer is assumed stochastic and unbiased (real RTN with data-dependent AbsMax scales is neither); columns are treated as i.i.d. samples in a way that sits awkwardly with the blockwise partitioning; and the FP error model (Theorem 2) assumes no subnormals/special values and ignores clipping of outliers. Optimality holds for the second-order surrogate objective, not the actual quantization loss, and the paper should be more careful in separating these claims.

The experimental evaluation is explicitly preliminary and limited in scope: layerwise loss is reported for a single layer (18th block) of a single model (Qwen3-8B); there is no perplexity evaluation; no comparison on LLM benchmarks against the strongest competing transforms (SpinQuant, QuaRot, FlatQuant are discussed in related work but never compared end-to-end); and the quantizer is plain RTN without integration with GPTQ-style error compensation, which limits practical relevance of the accuracy numbers.

Inference-time computational overhead is not measured. WUSH applies a distinct dense d×d non-orthogonal transform per block to activations at inference (Eq. 25), unlike Hadamard which reuses one fast structured transform; the paper acknowledges this complicates kernels but provides no latency/throughput numbers, so it is impossible to judge whether the accuracy gains survive a cost-benefit analysis.

There is an unexplained theory-practice gap: for INT4, WUS (the theory-only variant without Hadamard) fails catastrophically on Q/K (loss .21 vs .0024), yet the INT analysis (Section 2.3) predicts U′=H is optimal only within a factor d^{o(1)}; the discussion in 3.2 addresses MXFP4 but not this large discrepancy for pure INT.

Reproducibility is weak: no code release is mentioned, calibration details (damping λ, sample selection) are only sketched, and the evaluation set (Platinumbench, LM Eval Harness subset) is not accompanied by seeds/variance for Table 2 despite WUSH's margins over baselines sometimes being small (e.g., NVFP4 on Llama-3.1-8B, where identity slightly beats WUSH).

The manuscript lacks a dedicated limitations section; honest discussion exists only partially via future work (kernel support, GPTQ integration), while other limitations (surrogate-objective optimality, i.i.d. assumptions, single-layer loss experiments, RTN-only quantizer) are underemphasized.

strengths: The core question is well motivated and clearly posed: if fixed data-agnostic transforms like the Hadamard are empirically effective for quantization, what is the data-aware optimum? This is a natural and interesting theoretical question that has not been formally answered in the quantization literature.

The derivation is largely self-contained and constructive: the reduction from the two-sided weight-activation problem to a one-sided problem (Eq. 8), the parameterization via SVD, and the chain of inequalities for the FP case (Eqs. 13-14) yielding an attained closed-form optimum are reasonably clean and verifiable.

The paper is honest that results are 'preliminary' and the future work section candidly identifies real limitations, including the per-block kernel overhead relative to reusable Hadamard rotations and the computational cost of non-orthogonal transforms.

The layer-loss experiments include useful ablations (identity, random rotation, Hadamard, WUS without Hadamard) and cover three relevant numerical formats (MXFP4, NVFP4, INT4), with WUSH showing consistent improvements over Hadamard on the measured objectives.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is far too thin to support the practical significance claims. Layer loss is evaluated on a single transformer block (the 18th) of a single model (Qwen3-8B) with only 32 calibration samples. The end-to-end evaluation uses only RTN quantization on four models and a narrow benchmark set; there is no integration with, or comparison against, established post-training methods (GPTQ, SpinQuant, QuaRot, QuIP#, FlatQuant), which are the actual methods practitioners would consider. The paper explicitly defers GPTQ integration to future work.

Efficiency is claimed in the abstract ('remains structured for efficient implementation') but never demonstrated. WUSH uses a distinct dense d×d non-orthogonal matrix per block applied to activations at inference time, which is substantially more expensive than a fast Hadamard transform (O(d log d)) and has no existing kernel support. No FLOPs, memory, or latency measurements are reported anywhere, and the conclusion itself admits this complicates kernel reuse and fusion. For a paper whose contribution is an alternative to Hadamard in a deployment-motivated setting, this omission is decisive.

The theoretical guarantees rest on strong and partly unverified assumptions: a stochastic unbiased quantizer (real RTN is deterministic), a first-order approximation that drops the cross term ε(T_W w)ᵀε(T_X x) in Eq. (7), i.i.d. column samples, block-independent loss approximation, and Gaussian/Laplacian tail assumptions for the INT case, whereas LLM activations are heavy-tailed. The claimed 'optimal for FP / asymptotically optimal for INT' results therefore hold under smoothings that may not describe practical quantizers well, and the INT result retains up to a factor-d gap. The paper asserts the problem reduction is consistent with T_W = T_X^{-⊤} but does not fully verify this.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code release is mentioned, the damping ratio λ is introduced in Algorithm 1 but its value and sensitivity are never reported or ablated, and no variance or seed information is given for the benchmark results in Table 2, where several margins over Hadamard (e.g., NVFP4 on Llama-3.1-8B: 75.28 vs 74.00, but WUSH trails identity-based quantization at 75.33) are small and could be within noise.

There is an unexplained anomaly in the central results: in Table 1, WUS is catastrophic for INT4 on Q, K, and Gate layers (e.g., .21268 vs .00557 for Hadamard), while WUSH performs well. This suggests the Hadamard backbone, not the data-aware component, is doing most of the work in some regimes, yet this is not analyzed. Similarly, the theory predicts no benefit from orthogonal transforms for ideal FP quantization (Section 2.2.3), which is at odds with the observed Hadamard gains for MXFP4 and the mixed NVFP4 results (Hadamard underperforms identity for NVFP4 in Table 1); the paper offers only qualitative post-hoc discussion.

Presentation issues: Figures 1-4 are illegibly small, with heatmap cell values unreadable; Table 2 has broken layout in the model column; there is no dedicated limitations section beyond the future-work paragraphs.

The inference-time treatment of the per-token activation transform (Eq. 25) requires q applied to T_hsuw(i)X(i) for every block, an unquantified runtime overhead that undermines the claim of practical applicability and is not analyzed even at a theoretical cost level.

strengths: Original and well-motivated theoretical contribution: the paper is the first to derive closed-form, data-aware (non-orthogonal) optimal blockwise linear transforms for joint weight-activation quantization, going beyond the prevailing heuristic use of fixed Hadamard rotations. The question 'in what sense can Hadamard be optimal, and what does data-awareness buy?' is clearly posed and answered.

The proof architecture is clean and layered: probabilistic reformulation of the block loss (Sec. 2.1), a smooth FP quantization error model (Thm 2) leading to an exact optimality result via Cauchy–Schwarz and Jensen inequalities (Eqs. 13–14), and an INT analysis using von Neumann's trace inequality and maximum inequalities for tail-bounded distributions (Eqs. 16–24, Appendix A). The derivation that orthogonality alone cannot reduce quantization error (Eq. 15) is an insightful result that explains observed empirical behavior.
The resulting algorithm (Algorithm 1) is simple, closed-form, calibration-based (no training), and reuses GPTQ-style Hessian computation, making it easy to slot into existing PTQ pipelines.

Experimental results are directionally convincing: WUSH consistently achieves the lowest layerwise loss across MXFP4, NVFP4, and INT4 (Table 1), and shows consistent accuracy gains over identity and Hadamard RTN across four models on LM Eval Harness (Table 2) and Platinumbench (Figs. 1–4), including large gains for MXFP4 (e.g., +4.7 points on Llama-3.1-8B). The paper also honestly interprets where theory and practice diverge (MXFP4 as an FP/INT hybrid).
Limitations and future work are discussed candidly (kernel support overhead of per-block transforms, GPTQ integration, simplified diagonal variants).
weaknesses: A gap between the 'provably optimal' claim and the assumptions: the theory requires (i) a stochastic, unbiased quantizer whereas RTN is deterministic; (ii) a first-order approximation that discards the second-order error term ε(Tw)ᵀε(Tx) in Eq. (7) without any bound on the discarded error; and (iii) zero-mean Gaussian/Laplacian data for the tightened INT bounds, which conflicts with the heavy-tailed outlier distributions that motivate the whole paper. The INT result is only optimality 'up to a d^o(1) factor', i.e., asymptotic, not exact. The abstract and conclusion present 'provably optimal' more strongly than the assumptions support.

The empirical evaluation is explicitly preliminary and lacks the most important baselines: no comparison with SpinQuant or FlatQuant (the existing data-aware/calibration-based transforms), QuaRot, or GPTQ-integrated pipelines. Without SpinQuant, the central selling point—closed-form data-awareness beating learned rotations—remains untested. INT4 is studied in the layer-loss analysis but absent from the end-to-end benchmark table (Table 2 covers only MXFP4/NVFP4).

The layer-loss study uses a single transformer block (18th block of Qwen3-8B), and the anomalous WUS/INT4 result (.21 vs .00239 for WUSH) — showing the Hadamard component is essential for INT — is unexplained despite its significance for the theory-practice relationship. No perplexity evaluation is reported.

Practicality of the method is under-examined. WUSH applies a distinct, non-orthogonal d×d dense matrix per block to activations at inference time, which conflicts with the claim that it 'remains structured for efficient implementation'; no wall-clock, memory, or kernel measurements are provided. The transform memory footprint (din² per layer vs. a single shared Hadamard) is not quantified.

Some derivations and notation need tightening: the decomposition of E[(A+B)²] into two terms in Eq. (7) implicitly assumes a vanishing cross-term that is not justified; Eq. (18)'s chain of inequalities and the d^o(1) gap claim in Eqs. (21)–(23) are loosely stated; typos (e.g., 'Thsuw', 'LLama') and an idiosyncratic naming scheme reduce polish.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, calibration hyperparameters (damping λ, clipping for INT4) are under-specified, and results are averaged over few runs/seed configurations without variance reporting for Table 2.
